item.title: Between Two Worlds: Navigating Modern Fatherhood
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Between Two Worlds: Navigating Modern Fatherhood

Many dads today feel more fulfilled, but also more overwhelmed.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Modern fathers are balancing old expectations with a new vision of connection, partnership, and presence.
  • Today's dads need support, too: Many carry invisible pressures around work, parenting, and family life.
  • Strength and vulnerability can coexist. Changing this norm takes patience and understanding.
Source: oppo-find-x5-pro/Unsplash

My husband and I bickered about our domestic load-sharing for many years. One time, after the dust settled from one of our skirmishes, he opened up, “You know, I think it’s because I just never saw my father getting involved with the home.”

My heart softened as it finally registered how baked-in these roles were for him. I was expecting my husband to effortlessly traverse between worlds, the one he inherited and the one I wanted us to create. A dose of compassion tamed my frustration. With more understanding, we began working together to make small changes in our home life that have since built greater harmony between us.

The domestic load is just one of many aspects of fatherhood, and masculinity, that has dramatically evolved, culminating in what has recently been coined as “the millennial dad.”

Millennial Dad

A "millennial dad" is a father born generally between 1981 and 1996. Many (not all) of these dads are changing what fatherhood looks like. Rather than being background providers showing up for the big milestones, more dads are also helping with bedtime, housework, school dropoffs, doctor's appointments, and even emotional conversations. Many seek a stronger partnership with their spouse.

Of course, the level of this change varies from family to family, man to man. Plenty of millennial dads, and moms, choose more traditional roles, and plenty of working parents both have all hands on deck at home. Further, more dads serve as primary caregivers than ever. In fact, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center, the number of stay-at-home dads has nearly doubled over the past three decades.

The Upsides—and Pressures—of Modern Fatherhood

Many of the millennial fathers I meet with light up about being actively involved with their children. They relish the deep bond they have formed and wouldn't want it any other way. Nonetheless, in the same breath I also hear how overwhelmed they feel, and how hard it is to be present amidst all the pressures. The pain that surfaces time and again is a persistent feeling of falling short despite working harder than ever.

Many men feel pressure to not only excel professionally and provide financially, but at the same time, be an attuned parent, show up for their marriage, and stay well physically and mentally.

Just as we should address the invisible mental load many mothers carry, the silent burdens that many fathers carry need to be acknowledged as well. This ranges from financial pressure to fears of failure, confusion about their role, and heartache from missing family moments due to work.

What should dads, and moms, keep in mind to navigate today's expanding definition of manhood and fatherhood?

Tips for Dads

  • Practice self-compassion. Let yourself be a student of life, growing as your children grow. When we are kind to ourselves, we are actually more likely to change and grow.
  • Aim for connection over perfection. Your children will remember how they feel being with you more than anything else.
  • Talk openly about your feelings and struggles. You will not only feel less alone, but model to your children the strength in being vulnerable.

Tips for Moms (Co-Parent)

  • Keep love at the center. We change best when feeling loved, not evaluated.

  • Let small changes matter. Focusing on growth versus outcome will give you a chance to grow too, and become more patient and trusting.

  • Awaken radical appreciation. Seeing the good takes more effort than seeing what's missing. Awakening appreciation is a powerful tool. It's good to have open expectations but also important to not let your expectations cloud the opportunity for embracing the good in what, and who, you have.

  • Encourage your spouse to open up, and listen with empathy. Men are often more inclined to feel shame for any kind of struggle, so the less you judge, the more likely he'll show vulnerability.

Tips for Couples

Two key elements make all the difference: connection and communication.

  • Prioritize your bond. It's so easy to get caught up in the day-to-day, but it's essential that you carve out time for just the two of you, even if brief. Make each other a priority. The small things like a warm hug make a difference. You each must know you are the most important person in each other's lives. That's why "Priority" insisted its way into my book, A Soulful Marriage, as Pillar 3.
  • Schedule calendar meetings. On a practical level, you'll need regular check-ins because a smaller conversation today prevents deeper resentments tomorrow. Calendar meetings are not sexy but they reduce conflict, which opens the gates for greater intimacy.

  • Customize, don't compare. The human mind naturally compares and seeks what others have. This robs us of the blessings right before our eyes. Be honest and real about what will work in your family, and the unique souls you've chosen to share life with.

Bigger Picture: A Spiritual Perspective

Strength and vulnerability can absolutely coexist. As author and co-director of the Kabbalah Centre, Monica Berg, says about fathers, "being strong doesn’t mean you can’t be gentle, kind, and empathetic." Fathers need to know that it's the consciousness they pass on to their children that matters most. Meaning, you pass on how you conduct yourself, believe in, and support your children. Children internalize how you treat their mother, handle stress, respond when wrong, and embrace change.

In sum

Living between worlds is not an easy road to traverse, and the impact on dads is often overlooked. While change is an essential element of living a truly fulfilling and meaningful life, we all travel lighter when we show compassion and appreciation to those we hold dear along the way.

item.title: Do Narcissists Know They're Narcissistic?
item.description:
Narcissism

Do Narcissists Know They're Narcissistic?

Most narcissists don't think their personality is a problem.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissists often know exactly how they behave and that others view them negatively.
  • They don’t see these traits as flaws—they may view them as useful assets.
  • They typically have no desire to change because they value status over being liked.
Source: Rosy / Bad Homburg / Germany from Pixabay

Narcissism, characterized by grandiose self-perceptions, attention-seeking, and a sense of entitlement, is damaging to relationships. Narcissism expert Keith Campbell describes it as "like a disease where the sufferers feel pretty good, but the people around them suffer." There is no shortage of discussion, in both popular media and academic research, on the deleterious effects narcissism has on interpersonal relationships, particularly over the long term.

If narcissists think they're great, does that mean they are unaware of the damage they're doing to others or the negative impressions they make? Are they blissfully ignorant of the harm and bad reputation they leave behind? Or are they aware of their own narcissism and know perfectly well how it affects others? Research suggests that they are very much aware of their narcissism, and they don't think it’s a problem.

Do Narcissists Know They're Narcissistic?

The answer to this question is a definitive "yes." The simplest evidence comes from psychologists who measure narcissism. Personality psychologists measure narcissistic traits in the general population and rarely focus on people with the clinical diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder. There are several personality questionnaires that measure these traits, and each questionnaire contains multiple items, so study participants can receive a score ranging from relatively low to relatively high in narcissistic traits. The most widely used measure is the Narcissistic Personality Inventory (NPI). In order to be more efficient, researchers developed the single-item narcissism scale, which asks participants to rate the extent to which the following statement is true of them: "I am a narcissist." (The researchers included a note to participants defining "narcissist" as egotistical, self-focused, and vain). In the study, participants who answered this single-item question also completed the longer NPI. The results showed that there was, in fact, a consistent, moderate correlation between participants' responses to this question and their NPI score. In short: if someone admits they are a narcissist, they usually are.

Multiple studies have shown that narcissistic individuals do, in fact, describe themselves as high in narcissistic qualities and behaviors. Those who score higher on narcissism scales rate themselves as more arrogant and more likely to exaggerate their skills. They also describe themselves as more condescending, more likely to brag, and more likely to criticize others. These self-perceptions also match reality. Studies show these opinions are shared by both people who are just meeting them, as well as people who know them well, such as friends and family members.

How Do Narcissists Perceive Themselves Compared to Others?

People with negative or problematic traits can be aware of these traits and can also realize that these qualities create difficulties for themselves or others. In fact, many people do actively want to change their personality for the better. What about narcissists?

In one study, participants rated how socially desirable narcissistic traits, such as arrogance, were (that is, do they have socially desirable consequences?), and how personally desirable they were (that is, do they have positive consequences for themselves)? Those high in narcissism didn't think these traits were particularly socially desirable—they were just as aware as anyone else that these traits can have a negative impact on others. However, those high in narcissism were more likely to see these traits as being good for themselves. They were also more likely to describe their ideal selves as higher on these traits—meaning they think it would be a good idea to be even more arrogant, condescending, and prone to bragging.

Narcissists Value Status Over Kindness

Studies that ask participants to rate themselves on a variety of interpersonal traits find that narcissists tend to perceive themselves as especially intelligent, extraverted, and physically attractive, and they tend to overestimate themselves on these traits compared to how others view them. However, they don't have particularly lofty views about how honest and kind they are.

One popular theory is that deep down inside, narcissists secretly feel inferior. But the evidence suggests otherwise. A clever study that used reaction time data to measure automatic, unconscious self-perceptions found that narcissists feel pretty good about themselves. And again, they tended to both consciously and unconsciously inflate their value on agentic traits like attractiveness, extraversion, and intelligence, but not interpersonal traits, like warmth and kindness.

Narcissists simply do not believe that being a nice person is that important. When they choose romantic partners, they put more emphasis on looks and status, relative to kindness, and are happiest when partners meet their standards in those areas. When they are asked about their life goals, they will prioritize wealth and fame, and are happiest when they achieve those goals. Those low in narcissism tend to be more satisfied in relationships with those who are kind and devoted and they are happier in life if they pursue goals like having fulfilling personal relationships and giving back to their community.

Narcissists often seem to know they are interpersonally unpleasant—but they also know those same traits help them gain status, which is what they truly care about. As far as they're concerned, it's a feature, not a bug.

item.title: Senior Cats: How to Keep Your Kitty Happy as They Age
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Senior Cats: How to Keep Your Kitty Happy as They Age

The small changes you can make to give your older cat a better life.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Cats are considered senior at age 10, and super senior from 15 years old.
  • Behavior changes in your older cat may be a sign of medical issues, so stay on top of vet visits.
  • Senior cats still need play and enrichment, so make time for play with a wand toy.

This year, my cat Melina turned 16. Her beautiful tortoiseshell coat is a little faded, but she still has a fierce personality, living up to the tortie stereotype. As an older cat, though, she needs a little extra care. So how can we help our senior kitties to be as happy as possible?

Cats are considered mature between 7 and 10 years of age, senior from 10 to 14 years, and super senior from 15 years. As cats get older, they experience physiological changes similar to those in people as they age. There is a lot that we can do to help make their lives better.

Stay on top of medical issues

Vet visits should be more frequent as cats get older. The Feline Veterinary Medical Association recommends that cats aged 10-15 years should have a wellness visit at their vet twice a year, becoming as often as every four months for cats over 15 (Ray et al 2021). That’s assuming they are healthy; if your cat has medical issues, more frequent visits may be needed.

Observe your cat in your home so that you can let the vet know of any changes you have seen. Pain due to problems such as degenerative joint disease or dental issues is more common in older cats. Ask yourself if they are still jumping up and down from furniture like they used to and if they still go up and down stairs the same as before. For example, do they still jump from a table to the floor? And if they do, do they put a paw down a table leg first to reduce the distance they are jumping? Do they still go to the top of their favourite cat tree? As well, ask yourself if their interactions with you are still the same as normal, and if they meow more at odd times like in the middle of the night. If you notice changes in your cat’s behavior, tell your vet.

Source: Heidi Bollich/Shutterstock

Changes to the environment for your senior cat

Some tweaks to the environment can help your senior cat to be more comfortable. Position a step or ramp to help them get to favourite high-up resting places like the sofa. Make sure that food and water bowls are accessible to them. Senior cats in particular may prefer a wider, lower bowl for their water. They may need litter boxes with a lower entrance that makes it easier for them to step in and out of them. Senior cats may also prefer a softer surface for scratching posts, so if you don’t already have a carpet scratching post, now is a good time to get one.

There are some guidelines for a cat’s environment called the five pillars (Ellis et al 2013). They are designed for every cat, so now is a good time to make sure that you are meeting those five pillars. This means having multiple resources for your cat (such as beds, litter boxes, food bowls, etc.) that are separated from each other. It means recognizing their excellent sense of smell, such as by not using strongly-scented cleaners near their litter box. It means ensuring that your interactions with your cat are positive and predictable. It means making sure that your cat has a safe space; and now that they are older, they may need steps or ramps to ensure that they can reach their safe space. And it means making sure that they still have opportunities for play and predatory behavior.

Interactions and play with your senior cat

But unfortunately it turns out that senior cats may engage less in play. One study found that super seniors play less with toys than senior and mature cats (Hoummady et al 2026). The favourite toy for all of these age groups is a wand toy (also known as a fishing rod toy). It’s possible that people think their older cat isn’t interested in play, but remember that opportunities for play and predatory behaviour is one of the five pillars. So it is important to still make time to play with your cat.

Senior and super-senior cats are also less likely to be fed via food puzzle toys (Hoummady et al 2026). This may in part be because older cats are more likely to be fed wet food, though you can still make them work for wet food by putting it in little bowls and hiding it for them to find. But it could also be that people find it more difficult to introduce new food puzzle toys for older cats. When giving your cat a new food puzzle toy, always make it super-easy for them, and put treats in it to get their interest. Watch them for signs of frustration and give them a helping hand if needed. Another way in which super senior and senior cats miss out compared to mature cats is in the provision of olfactory enrichment such as catnip and silvervine.

Older cats are more likely to need help with grooming and to have their claws clipped. It’s a good reason to ensure that cats of any age are used to being brushed and to having their paws handled, in case they need help with this later on. Of course, some long-haired cats may need regular brushing throughout their lives.

If you struggle to get your cat to the vet, it’s worth knowing that it’s never too late to teach your cat to like their cat carrier. Cats can learn at any age, and training with positive reinforcing can be a fun activity for them. If you need help, there’s a plan to teach your cat to like their carrier at the end of my book Purr. Remember to keep the cat carrier in a room that your cat uses often. Ideally, it will become a place where they can lounge and relax.

As always, see your veterinarian if you have concerns.

item.title: Sobriety and Recovery: It’s Important to Know the Difference
item.description:
Addiction

Sobriety and Recovery: It’s Important to Know the Difference

Defining sobriety and recovery, which shouldn't be used interchangeably.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Sobriety and recovery are not synonymous; they describe fundamentally different things.
  • Recovery spans health, housing, purpose, and community—not just substance use or the absence of it.
  • Treating sobriety as recovery can cause clinicians to miss people who need care.

It’s likely that in any treatment center, recovery community organization, or peer support meeting, you will hear the words sobriety and recovery used as if they mean the same thing. They’re actually quite different. The conflation between the two is so common that even clinicians, payers, and policy documents slip between the two without flagging the difference. This imprecision matters, because the two words describe entirely different things, and treating them as synonyms shapes how care is delivered, how progress is measured, and how people understand their own change.

Whether someone is pursuing total abstinence, a harm reduction approach, medication-assisted treatment, a "California sober" framework, or partial recovery, the distinction applies. Sobriety and recovery are related concepts, but they are not interchangeable ones.

Sobriety, Unlike Recovery, Is a Behavioral State

Sobriety refers to a person's relationship with a substance or set of substances at a given point in time. It is, at its core, a behavioral descriptor. Someone is sober when they are not currently using the substance in question, or when their use has changed in a defined and measurable way.

Sobriety can take several forms, and each is a legitimate way of describing a person's substance use status:

  • Total abstinence from all psychoactive substances.
  • Substance-specific abstinence, in which a person stops using one drug while continuing others (the colloquial “California sober” often falls here, typically meaning abstinence from alcohol and harder substances while continuing cannabis or psychedelics).
  • Reduced or controlled use, consistent with harm reduction frameworks, where the goal is decreased frequency, quantity, or risk rather than full cessation.
  • Medication-supported sobriety, in which medications such as buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone stabilize the person and eliminate or reduce illicit substance use.

What unites these forms is that sobriety can be observed and measured. It can be confirmed through toxicology, self-report, or behavioral tracking. It has a start date. It can be interrupted by a return to use. It is, in clinical terms, a state, not a process.

This is why someone can be sober and still be unwell and/or suffering. Removing a substance does not, on its own, repair the conditions that made the substance attractive in the first place. A person can be six months without a drink and still be isolated, dysregulated, financially unstable, in conflict with family, and unable to work. They are sober. They are not, by most working definitions, in recovery.

Recovery Is a Process of Change

Recovery is a longer, broader concept. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) defines recovery as a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach their full potential. The definition is intentionally wide, because recovery is not confined to substance use behavior.

Recovery touches multiple domains at once:

  • Health: including physical health, mental health, and management of any co-occurring conditions.
  • Home: meaning a stable and safe place to live.
  • Purpose: through meaningful daily activity such as work, school, caregiving, creative pursuits, or community involvement.
  • Community: meaning relationships and social networks that provide support, friendship, love, and hope.

Recovery is not a status someone achieves on a particular date. It unfolds over months and years, it is non-linear, and it includes setbacks. It involves identity change, the rebuilding of relationships, the development of coping skills, the formation of new routines, and often the reconstruction of a sense of self that substance use displaced or obscured. Recovery can begin while a person is still using, and it can continue long after substance use has stopped being a daily concern.

Importantly, recovery does not require abstinence in every framework. Many evidence-based and lived-experience definitions accommodate recovery with continued use, partial recovery, and recovery in remission. A person on long-term medication-assisted treatment who is working, parenting, and stable is in recovery, regardless of whether they meet a strict abstinence definition. A person who has reduced alcohol use to non-problematic levels, repaired family relationships, and returned to consistent functioning is also in recovery, even if they are not sober in the abstinence sense.

Why the Distinction Matters for Providers

Confusing the two terms produces predictable problems.

When sobriety is treated as the same thing as recovery, abstinence becomes the only marker of progress. This narrows what counts as success and disqualifies the substantial gains people make through harm reduction, medication-assisted treatment, and partial recovery pathways. It also obscures the opposite problem: people who are abstinent but functionally deteriorating, whose distress goes unaddressed because their toxicology is clean.

When recovery is treated as the same thing as sobriety, the work of building a life is reduced to the work of avoiding a substance. The result is a thin definition of progress that does not capture the actual changes recovery requires, and that leaves people unprepared for what comes after the substance is no longer the central problem.

The cleanest way to hold the distinction is this. Sobriety describes what a person is doing with a substance. Recovery describes who a person is becoming and how they are living. The two often travel together. They do not always, and they are not the same.

How the Terms Sobriety and Recovery Relate in Practice

Sobriety and recovery interact in several recognizable patterns:

  • Sober and in recovery. The person has changed their substance use and is also building health, purpose, stability, and connection.
  • Sober but not in recovery. Sometimes called “dry” in peer language. Substance use has stopped or reduced, but the underlying dysregulation, isolation, or instability remains.
  • In recovery but not fully sober. The person is rebuilding a life across multiple domains while continuing some level of substance use, often in a harm reduction or medication-assisted framework.
  • Neither sober nor in recovery. Active use without meaningful behavioral or life-domain change.

All four patterns exist. All four show up in clinical practice, in peer communities, and in the data. Recognizing them requires using the right word for the right concept.

Why Does Language Precision Matter?

Precision in language is not pedantry in this field. It shapes treatment plans, outcome measures, insurance authorizations, public messaging, and the way people describe their own progress to themselves. Sobriety and recovery are both important. They are not the same. Saying so clearly, and consistently, is part of the work.

item.title: Why You Adapt to Things You Never Intended to Accept
item.description:
Authenticity

Why You Adapt to Things You Never Intended to Accept

Our lives are shaped by the small compromises we make as we move through our days.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Small compromises rarely feel like betrayals. They feel practical.
  • Adaptation protects us and can also control us.
  • Integrity doesn’t disappear in one dramatic collapse; it fades with softened boundaries and edited truths.
  • The space between stimulus and response determines authorship.

Several weeks ago, during the latest escalation involving Iran, I found myself on a Zoom call discussing an upcoming speaking engagement. The conversation involved the perfectly ordinary discussions of calendars, travel logistics, and deadlines. At one point, I glanced at my phone and saw a message from a friend in Tehran who had recently been released from detention by the morality police. He began by expressing the hope that the message itself would get through, given the internet blackout and power outages. He wasn't lamenting the war so much as the lack of anything that mattered to our people, even the list of negotiation demands by either side. A few seconds later, I was back to discussing schedules. "What time did you say that Monday morning?" "Oh yes, that can work."

The contrast felt surreal. How can a conference schedule occupy any space amidst the grim realities of my home country, where I'd lived as a child and where tons of family and friends still live? It's remarkable how we can inhabit two worlds at once. One part of us continues answering emails, making dinner, and attending meetings. Another part understands that events of enormous consequence are unfolding in the background.

As days passed, I noticed a different question emerging. It wasn't whether I cared. Unquestionably, I did. A great deal, in fact. It was whether I was actively choosing where my attention, energy, and life would go, or whether circumstance was quietly choosing for me. Recent events in Iran reminded many people that history can change suddenly. Yet lives are shaped by the thousands of ordinary decisions made while we're busy adapting to whatever is happening around us.

Exploring Adaptation and Agency in Modern Life

The question itself stayed with me long after the news cycle moved on. In fact, it eventually became the subject of a recent TEDx talk I gave on adaptation, agency, and the subtle ways circumstances shape us when we're not paying attention. What interested me most wasn't the crisis itself, but how quickly human beings learn to live alongside almost anything.

Human beings have an extraordinary capacity to adapt. That capacity allows us to survive war, political oppression, social tension, professional pressure, and the ordinary turbulence of relationships. The nervous system recalibrates to keep functioning, and it does so with impressive intelligence. Over time, what once startled us begins to feel manageable as the intolerable becomes familiar.

Small compromises enter through that same door of familiarity. They rarely arrive as dramatic betrayals of character. They appear as practicality, maturity, or realism and present themselves as a reasonable effort to maintain harmony, conserve energy, or keep life moving smoothly. We don’t wake up intending to abandon our standards. We wake up intending to get through the day, to meet our obligations, to preserve our relationships, to stay steady in the face of complexity. In that pursuit, subtle adjustments accumulate.

A professional accepts a project that doesn't quite align with her values because it seems easier than declining. A year later, she finds herself doing work she never intended to do. A couple avoids a difficult conversation because the timing never feels right. Months later, they are living with assumptions neither of them consciously chose. A parent postpones a dream, a creative project, or a personal ambition until life becomes less demanding. The years pass more quickly than expected. Thus, even if no one decision feels transformative, the accumulation is.

Ordinary Choices Shape Identity

This is one of the great paradoxes of adulthood. We tend to imagine that our lives will be shaped by dramatic moments: a marriage, a divorce, a promotion, a move across the country. In reality, identity is often formed through decisions so ordinary that we barely notice that we're making them.

The Stoics understood this well. Marcus Aurelius repeatedly reminded himself that character is built in seemingly insignificant moments. Not in grand declarations, but in daily responses. Not in extraordinary circumstances, but in ordinary ones repeated over time. Modern psychology arrives at a similar conclusion. Researchers studying habit formation and behavioral inertia have found that people frequently continue existing patterns simply because those patterns already exist. The familiar exerts a gravitational pull. What we repeatedly tolerate, repeat, postpone, or prioritize gradually becomes the framework through which we live.

This is why the interval between stimulus and response matters so profoundly.

Within that interval lies the faculty of choice, the capacity to determine whether an action aligns with one's values or merely reduces immediate discomfort. In relationships, this interval might be the breath taken before laughing at a remark that unsettles you. In professional settings, it might be the pause before agreeing to a decision that conflicts with your judgment. Online, it may appear as the moment of hesitation before scrolling past something that warrants deeper attention.

When that governing space is bypassed, habits and circumstances begin writing our story for us. Decisions become reflexive, guided by convenience, avoidance, or momentum. When that space is inhabited deliberately, even briefly, a different quality of authorship emerges. One begins to ask whether silence reflects wisdom or fear, whether flexibility reflects generosity or gradual self-erasure, whether a decision serves a long-term vision or merely solves a short-term discomfort.

Compromise is woven into adult life. Intimacy requires accommodation, and cooperation demands adjustment. A rigid refusal to bend would fracture most relationships. The challenge arises when adjustments consistently move in one direction, narrowing expression, lowering expectations, or muting conscience without conscious acknowledgment. Over time, the cumulative effect of these small permissions can reshape a life more powerfully than any singular dramatic event.

Resilience through adaptation retains its virtue when it’s chosen with awareness and integrity. But how do we distinguish between protecting the capacity to act while refusing accommodations that redraw our boundaries? That distinction can’t be outsourced to circumstance alone because it's also inexplicably tied to our own ongoing reflection. The small compromises that change us seldom feel dramatic. They feel reasonable because they’re tethered to legitimate needs for safety, harmony, and efficiency.

Yet reasonableness alone doesn’t guarantee alignment. A life shaped primarily by unexamined comfort can slowly distance us from earlier convictions.

The Negotiation Between Circumstance and Conscience

I'll never forget receiving that message from Tehran. How my heart sank while my words kept finalizing my conference details. While governments negotiate over borders, sanctions, missiles, and power, every ordinary person is left to negotiate something else entirely: whether they'll become the person their circumstances demand or the person their conscience requires.

The outcome of that negotiation rarely makes headlines, but it's the one that determines the course of a life. It's also why I keep returning to the question, both in my writing and in recent public talks: How do we adapt without surrendering authorship of our own lives? The answer is rarely found in dramatic moments. More often, it emerges through the quiet decisions we make long before circumstances force our hand.
